text: Section 9 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 details the absolute grounds for refusal of trademark registration. Under Section 9(1)(b), trademarks which consist exclusively of signs or indications which may serve in trade to designate the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, values, geographical origin or the time of production of the goods or rendering of the service cannot be registered. In the context of Ayurvedic products, generic formulation names (e.g., 'Chawanprash' or 'Triphala') or purely descriptive Sanskrit terms for botanical ingredients cannot be exclusively trademarked by a single enterprise unless long-standing commercial use establishes acquired distinctiveness under the proviso to Section 9(1).

Section 4 of the Designs Act, 2000 prohibits the registration of certain industrial designs. It states that a design shall not be registered if it is not new or original, or if it has been disclosed to the public anywhere in India or in any other country by publication in tangible form or by use prior to the filing date, or if it is not significantly distinguishable from known designs or combinations of known designs. For Ayurvedic enterprises, proprietary bottle shapes, cosmetic jar containers, or traditional applicator tools can only secure design protection if the visual shape and configuration possess distinct aesthetic novelty rather than standard functional packaging long used in traditional medicine trade.

Under Section 13 of the Copyright Act, 1957, copyright subsists throughout India in original literary, dramatic, musical, and artistic works, as well as cinematograph films and sound recordings. For Ayurvedic commercial ventures, copyright protects original label artwork, custom package illustration designs, brand slogans, and original promotional literature. However, copyright does not extend to the underlying ancient Ayurvedic formulations, public domain Sanskrit shlokas, or traditional remedy recipes documented in authoritative texts listed under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act.

Section 39 of the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001 (PPV&FR Act) safeguards the rights of farmers regarding plant genetic resources. Section 39(1)(iv) explicitly guarantees that a farmer shall be deemed to be entitled to save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share or sell his farm produce including seed of a variety protected under this Act in the same manner as he was entitled heretofore, provided that the farmer shall not be entitled to sell branded seed of a variety protected under this Act. This ensures indigenous communities and traditional cultivators retain unrestricted rights to harvest and trade raw medicinal plants and traditional landraces used in Ayurvedic formulations.

text: Regulation 2 of the Food Safety and Standards (Ayurveda Aahara) Regulations, 2022 defines 'Ayurveda Aahara' as food prepared in accordance with the recipes, ingredients, and processes described in the authoritative books of Ayurveda listed under Schedule A of the regulations. It explicitly excludes Ayurvedic drugs or proprietary medicines under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, cosmetics, Schedule E-1 toxic herbs, metal/bhasma ingredients, and routine daily agricultural staples. Manufacturers of Ayurveda Aahara must comply with strict FSSAI labelling rules, mandatory prior approval for non-Schedule A additives, and clear declarations distinguishing these wellness foods from therapeutic medicines.

text: Article 27 of the TRIPS Agreement (WTO) governs patentable subject matter across international jurisdictions. Article 27(1) mandates that patents shall be available for any inventions, whether products or processes, in all fields of technology, provided they are new, involve an inventive step, and are capable of industrial application. Article 27(3)(a) allows WTO member states to exclude from patentability diagnostic, therapeutic, and surgical methods for the treatment of humans or animals, while Article 27(3)(b) permits exclusions for plants and animals. This international baseline allows member nations like India to bar patents on traditional medicinal knowledge and basic plant extracts while permitting patents on genuinely novel isolated active compounds.

Article 15 of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) establishes international standards for access to genetic resources and fair and equitable benefit sharing. Reaffirming the sovereign rights of States over their natural resources, Article 15(1) confirms that national governments hold authority to determine access to genetic resources subject to domestic legislation. Article 15(4) and 15(5) require that access be on Mutually Agreed Terms (MAT) and subject to the Prior Informed Consent (PIC) of the contracting party providing such resources. Foreign entities utilizing Indian medicinal flora for commercial bioprospecting or pharmaceutical development must comply with these international CBD principles as implemented through India's National Biodiversity Authority.

Article 5 of the Nagoya Protocol on Access to Genetic Resources and the Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits Arising from their Utilization operationalizes Article 15 of the CBD. Article 5(1) mandates that benefits arising from the utilization of genetic resources, as well as subsequent applications and commercialization, shall be shared in a fair and equitable way with the country of origin providing such resources upon mutually agreed terms (MAT). Furthermore, Article 5(5) requires member parties to implement policy measures to ensure that benefits arising from the utilization of traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources held by indigenous and local communities are fairly shared with those communities.

Article 3 of the WIPO Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge (adopted 24 May 2024) introduces a mandatory international patent disclosure requirement. Where a claimed invention in a patent application is materially based on genetic resources, applicants must disclose the country of origin or source of those genetic resources. Where the claimed invention is materially based on traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources, the applicant must disclose the indigenous people or local community who provided the traditional knowledge. This landmark 2024 treaty provides an international legal mechanism to detect bioprospecting and prevent wrongful patent grants based on traditional Ayurvedic knowledge.

text: Article 3 and Article 15 of the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) govern the filing of international patent applications and the international search procedure. Under Article 3, an international application filed under the PCT has the effect of a regular national application in designated contracting states. Article 15 mandates that each international application be subjected to an International Search Report (ISR) carried out by an International Searching Authority (ISA). International patent examiners reference prior-art databases—including India's Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL)—during the PCT search phase to identify prior publication of traditional Ayurvedic herbal remedies worldwide.

Articles 2 and 3 of the Madrid Agreement / Protocol Concerning the International Registration of Marks govern the Madrid System administered by WIPO. Applicants who have filed or registered a trademark in their home office (such as the Indian Trade Marks Registry) can secure international trademark protection across up to 130 countries by filing a single international application in one language with one set of fees. This enables Indian Ayurvedic brands expanding globally to protect their commercial trade names and product branding seamlessly across multiple international target markets.

Articles 4 and 5 of the Hague Agreement Concerning the International Registration of Industrial Designs enable applicants to register industrial container and packaging designs in multiple countries through a single international application filed with WIPO. For Ayurvedic product manufacturers seeking to export novel proprietary dispensers, cosmetic jar packaging, or ergonomic applicator bottles, the Hague System provides centralized international design protection without needing separate individual national design filings in every target country.

Article 3 of the Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposit of Microorganisms for the Purposes of Patent Procedure requires contracting states that allow or require the deposit of microorganisms for patent prosecution to recognize a deposit made with any International Depositary Authority (IDA). For biotechnology and advanced Ayurvedic formulations involving specific probiotic bacterial strains, fermented bio-extracts (like traditional Asava/Arishta micro-fermentation), or microbial enzyme catalysts, a single deposit with a recognized IDA satisfies biological disclosure requirements across all Budapest member states.
